clue.text: Conclude to dress for cold weather

blocks.note: first meaning: bring a meeting or matter to an end
second meaning: put on warm layers before going out

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like one instruction, as if finishing means getting your coat on; the two halves are separate senses of one phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both finishing off business and bundling yourself in warm clothing against winter chill.

clue.text: Bird baked in pie now? Good

indicators.note: baking transforms what goes into the oven, so the letters come out changed in form

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the punctuation

explanation.surface: Someone tries a pie with a bird baked into it and declares it good.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and full stop split the fodder in the surface, but the letters run straight across: pie, now and good are all shuffled together.
explanation.definitionFit: The wood pigeon is a common large European dove, often shot as game and eaten in pies.

clue.text: Most of description of lorry is clear

indicators.note: most of something is all but a little of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a lorry with a cab and trailer joined by a pivot is described this way

explanation.surface: Someone praises a lorry description as largely lucid.
explanation.walkthrough: An articulated lorry is the British term for a tractor-trailer or semi; the D is the letter cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Articulate speech or writing is expressed fluently and coherently, so easy to understand.

clue.text: Peacekeepers deployed: that's not seen on Facebook?

blocks.note: the United Nations sends peacekeeping forces
troops deployed somewhere are posted there

explanation.surface: Peacekeeping troops have been sent out, but nobody has shared the news on social media.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: a post is something put on social media, so content never put up there is the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Material not shared as a status update or message on a social network has never been put up online.

clue.text: Over-hasty – and late!

blocks.note: first meaning: informal British, acting too soon
second meaning: former, as in 'the late chairman'

explanation.walkthrough: Hasty and late look like opposites, which is the joke the italic 'and' leans on; late here means former, not tardy.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the word describes someone jumping the gun, and formally it means prior or former holder of a post.

clue.text: Statement about antenatal position

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
the presentation is the way a baby lies in the womb before birth, such as breech

explanation.surface: A midwife issues a statement on how a baby is lying before birth.
explanation.walkthrough: Presentation is the obstetric term for which part of the baby will emerge first.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal account or claim made to an authority, as in making representations to a council, is a kind of statement.

clue.text: Fade out with loose description of a lorry?

blocks.note: a van is a smaller goods vehicle, close enough to a lorry, hence the question mark
the suffix -ish describes something only roughly

explanation.surface: A vague account of a truck seems to fade from memory.
explanation.walkthrough: Something lorry-ish is van-ish: the clue reads the answer as an adjective meaning roughly like a goods vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: To disappear suddenly or gradually from sight is to drop out of view entirely.

clue.text: Restriction for darts players getting round: revolutionary!

blocks.note: O is round in shape
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: Darts players get a round in and a radical rule is imposed.
explanation.walkthrough: In darts, a pub game hugely popular in Britain, the oche is the line on the floor that throwers must stand behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Players may not step over this marked throwing line, so it limits how close they stand to the board.

clue.text: Returned symbol of love, being cross

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Eros is the Greek god of love, often shown as a winged archer

explanation.surface: A rejected love token comes back, leaving the giver annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: The statue of Eros in London's Piccadilly Circus makes the god a familiar emblem of love.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal American and British use, feeling aggrieved or irritated is the same as being angry.

clue.text: Ginsberg, Kerouac etc all in reproduction

blocks.note: all in is British slang for exhausted, as is beat
generation is the producing of offspring

explanation.surface: The Beat writers are all included in some reprinted edition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All in' looks like it means everyone is included, but it is a single adjective for worn out.
explanation.definitionFit: Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac were leading figures in the 1950s American literary movement of that name.

clue.text: Terrible couplet, being four times greater?

definitions.note: four times a couplet's two, i.e. eightfold

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad state, so these letters are mangled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A poor two-line verse is pretentiously claimed to be worth four times as much.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition only works against the fodder: a couplet has two lines, and four times two is eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Octuple means eightfold, which is four times the pair of lines in a couplet.

clue.text: Creature seen in Japan? Thereabouts

indicators.note: what is seen in a place is visible inside it, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: the end of the country's name runs into the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A traveller asks whether some animal lives in Japan, and gets a vague answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the surface in two, but the letters run on across it.
explanation.definitionFit: A panther is a big cat, a leopard or jaguar, so a wild animal is a fair general description.

clue.text: Streetscape redesigned for athletic types

indicators.note: a redesign rearranges the parts of something into a new layout

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A town remodels its streets to suit runners and joggers.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the single long word is used, which makes the anagram easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Pacemakers in a race run at the front to set the speed for other runners.

clue.text: 'So any bread prepared?' 'It's completely devoid of moisture'

indicators.note: preparing food means working the ingredients into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: One person asks if bread has been made; the other complains it is parched.
explanation.walkthrough: The dialogue punctuation splits fodder from definition: the question supplies the letters, the reply is the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The simile likens something parched to an old bleached skeleton, meaning totally without water.

clue.text: Issues bids suspiciously, wanting funds

indicators.note: acting suspiciously means behaving oddly, so the letters behave out of their usual order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone places dodgy bids at auction because they need money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funds' looks like a noun for money wanted; it is a verb meaning pays for.
explanation.definitionFit: A body that pays part of the cost of something to support it is financing it.

clue.text: Bond film's aged fellow (so says Spooner)

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: aged is olden and a fellow is a guy; move the G sound to the front

explanation.surface: A Bond movie features an elderly man.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word has no opening consonant, so swapping the starts just moves the G from the second word to the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1995 James Bond film starring Pierce Brosnan is named after Ian Fleming's Jamaican home.

clue.text: Tongue stuffing in bulghur dumplings

indicators.note: stuffing sits inside what holds it, so the letters are found within the words

blocks.note: the end of the grain spills into the start of the pastry

explanation.surface: A tongue filling inside dumplings made with cracked wheat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' sounds like the meat in the filling; it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan, and tongue is a common synonym for language.

clue.text: Giggles, seeing chocolate bar

blocks.note: first meaning: suppressed, sniggering laughs
second meaning: the peanut and caramel brand name

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is someone laughing at a confectionery bar; the brand name is also a plural noun for smothered laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-stifled sly laughs are another word for chuckles, and the Mars brand candy bar shares the name.

clue.text: Holy Roman Emperor succeeding Berengar VIII in Rome

blocks.note: first meaning: the first German king of that name took the Italian crown from Berengar II in 961
second meaning: the Italian word for eight

explanation.walkthrough: The Roman numeral looks like a regnal number for Berengar; it is the number eight, said in Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: Several German rulers named Otto were crowned emperor, and the same word is the Italian numeral eight.

clue.text: Son among schoolboys who live by Baltic Sea?

definitions.note: a clause for 'people who live', standing for a plural noun

indicators.note: to be among a group is to be surrounded by it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: pupils at Eton College, the famous English boys' boarding school
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A boy at an elite school among pupils who live near the Baltic.
explanation.walkthrough: Schoolboys in crosswords are very often from Eton, England's best-known public school; the son goes in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a country on the eastern Baltic coast, so its citizens are people living there.

clue.text: Go sew?

blocks.note: first meaning: go somewhere
second meaning: mend, as sewing fixes torn clothes

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and a question mark: each is a separate sense of one verb, the first a formal word for taking yourself off somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to betake oneself to a place, formally, and to mend something broken or torn.

clue.text: Stationery item seen in basic dental reshaping

indicators.note: reshaping gives something a new form, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An office supply turns up in simple orthodontic work, as rubber bands do on braces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen in' usually signals a hidden word, but here it only links; the letters are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber loop for holding papers together is an office supply kept on a desk with pens and clips.

clue.text: Space to secure boat that's capsized

indicators.note: a capsized vessel is upside down, and in a down clue that turns the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: to moor is to tie up a vessel

explanation.surface: Room is needed to tie up a boat that has overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capsized' fits a down clue neatly: the word is flipped from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Room in the sense of available area or capacity, as in 'no room to move', is spare space.

clue.text: PM, in total twice, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: opening letter
opening letter
the opening letter of total, taken twice

explanation.surface: A question about how many times a prime minister held office.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition word also starts the wordplay; Pitt the Younger was twice Prime Minister, which gives the clue its double meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: William Pitt the Elder and his son the Younger both served as British Prime Minister.

clue.text: Old outfit: is Everyman making many creases?

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a rig is an outfit of clothes
the setter is I, and 'is I' becomes 'am I' in the question form

explanation.surface: The setter wonders whether an old suit is getting badly crumpled.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves by name; Everyman stands for I, and the verb shifts to agree.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese paper art folds a sheet repeatedly, so the activity is all about folding.

clue.text: Following fashion, coolest cats

indicators.note: following a fashion means remaking yourself in a new style, so the letters are restyled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The trendiest hipsters, the coolest cats, follow every fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coolest cats' reads as slang for hip people; cats is the literal definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild feline of the Americas, a member of the cat family.

clue.text: Ageing mathematician pursuing degree

indicators.note: to pursue is to come after, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: Master of Arts
Alan Turing, the British mathematician and codebreaker

explanation.surface: An elderly academic is studying for another qualification.
explanation.walkthrough: The mathematician comes first in the clue but second in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Growing older, or developing over time like wine or cheese, is becoming more mature.

clue.text: Archipelagos may be full of these holes, we're told

definitions.text: Archipelagos may be full of these

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken rather than seeing it written

blocks.note: eyelets are small holes for laces or cord

explanation.surface: A claim that island chains are riddled with holes.
explanation.walkthrough: The S in the answer is silent, so it sounds just like the small reinforced holes in shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: An archipelago is a group of islands, many of them tiny, so small islands fill it.
